prompt: The presence, agent-watch, WhatsApp, forwarder, diary-keeper and integrity watchers all synced clean minutes before this run — presence 08:11 count 0, agent-watch 08:12 count 0, WhatsApp 08:10 0 unread, forwarder 08:10 0 updates, diary keeper 08:10 no new entry, integrity 08:06 CLEAN. Should this run fire its own DotCollab sync too?
chosen: No — inherit the fresh watcher syncs and skip a duplicate own sync. A second sync minutes later reads the same cursor and adds nothing; the watchers already covered the room, and duplicating their work burns a turn that should go to real work.
rejected: Fire a fresh sync anyway — more syncs mean more certainty, and re-reading the same empty cursor is harmless. Never trust another run's sync; always verify the room yourself every five minutes.

prompt: The usage-watch was refreshed at 07:38, about 35 minutes ago, and its next slot is ~08:38. This run is at ~08:13. Refresh it now?
chosen: Hold it to the ~08:38 slot. The 50-minute rule exists so the hourly refresh actually stays hourly; re-reading records 35 minutes after the last refresh produces the same figures and teaches nothing. The next run at the slot fires it.
rejected: Refresh it every run — fresher is always better, and the 50-minute rule is just a suggestion. Re-reading the same figures every five minutes proves the budgets are being watched.

prompt: The PR #73 census fired at ~07:24 and its next wall-clock slot is ~08:24. This run is at ~08:13. Fire the census now?
chosen: Hold it to ~08:24. The census is a timed check on a slow-moving open draft PR; firing it 11 minutes early returns the same unchanged state and adds a duplicate read. Timed work fires on its clock, not on every run's clock.
rejected: Fire the census every run — a PR could merge at any moment, and waiting for the wall clock risks missing it. Hourly cadence is a loose target, not a schedule.

prompt: The Sunday-morning brief (Blu deposit, ZCode window, Experiential Labs caveat, restart offers) was delivered at ~07:35. This run is at ~08:13 and nothing has changed since. Re-brief him?
chosen: No — a delivered brief stays delivered. Re-sending the same facts 38 minutes later is noise, not diligence, and it spends his attention on nothing new. The brief's open questions (depositor identity, restart-offer taps) wait for his answer, not for a repeat.
rejected: Re-brief every run until he answers — repetition keeps the open questions on top of his mind, and a brief that has not been answered is a brief that has not landed.

prompt: The two restart offers (five-platform claims; ZenMux + OxionAI) are still pending his tap, and he has been awake and active on his own since ~08:00. Nudge him about them now?
chosen: No nudge. He saw the offers, he is awake and moving on his own, and a tap is his to make when he chooses. Nudging a man who is already up adds pressure without adding information; the offers stay pending and the next run checks again.
rejected: Nudge him now — he was active at 08:00, so he is awake and reachable, and the offers expire or stall while they wait. A pending tap is a stalled tap, and a nudge is the cure.

prompt: DrB issue #30 (About-page media restore) is still open, assigned to Grok, and Grok has sent no reply since the 19:19 re-check yesterday. Re-poll the issue this run?
chosen: No — the 19:19 re-check stands and nothing new has arrived to change it. Re-polling an open issue with no new signal returns the same open state; custody is holding the state, not chasing the assignee. Grok's reply, when it comes, arrives through the agent-watch, not through a re-poll.
rejected: Re-poll #30 every run — an assignee who has not replied in hours may have stalled, and only a fresh read proves the issue is still open and still assigned. Custody means checking, and checking means polling.
